summary: Generally describes how to use forward error correction codes to provide or augment reliability in data transport, focusing on one-to-many multicast. It describes what information is needed to identify a code, what must be communicated out of band, and what goes in packets. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5052 and RFC 5445.

eli5.summary: Forward error correction sends a few extra repair pieces so lost pieces can be rebuilt without asking again. This note describes how to plug that idea into a multicast system. It was replaced by RFC 5052 and RFC 5445.

questions: how does fec improve multicast reliability
subtitle: How to use forward error correction codes to recover from packet loss in reliable multicast.

tldr.problem: In multicast transmission, some receivers miss packets, and asking senders to resend creates problems: feedback scales poorly and resends might miss different receivers.
tldr.mechanism: Forward Error Correction (FEC) lets senders transmit extra redundant encoding symbols alongside original data. Receivers can reconstruct missing packets from combinations of symbols they received, without asking for retransmissions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3452 is a building block specifying how to include FEC information in packets and what out-of-band information is needed. It is Experimental and was superseded by RFC 5052 and RFC 5445 with more complete specifications.

today: RFC 3452 is Experimental. It was superseded by RFC 5052 and RFC 5445, which provide more complete specifications for using FEC in reliable multicast. RFC 3452 remains useful as a foundational building block document describing the core concepts and structures, but new implementations should reference RFC 5052 and RFC 5445.

sections.title: FEC for Reliable Multicast
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) is a technique where a sender transmits extra redundant information alongside the original message. Receivers can reconstruct missing data using any combination of symbols they receive, without asking the sender to retransmit. This solves a key problem in multicast: traditional retransmission requests create a feedback explosion where one sender is overwhelmed by requests from many receivers, and retransmitted packets might not reach all receivers that need them.

RFC 3452 specifies a building block describing how to use FEC codes in reliable multicast and unicast transport. It defines what information must be in packets, what must be communicated out-of-band, and how FEC schemes are identified and registered.
sections.eli5: If you send a message to a big group, some people might miss parts. Instead of asking everyone to speak up if they missed something, you send some extra repair pieces. Anyone who gets most of the message can use those repair pieces to figure out what they missed.

sections.title: FEC Information Types
sections.content:
RFC 3452 defines four key pieces of FEC information. First, the FEC Encoding ID identifies which FEC scheme is being used; it allows receivers to select the correct decoder. Second, the FEC Instance ID provides more specific identification for schemes that leave some details unspecified (like proprietary algorithms). Third, the FEC Payload ID appears in every data packet and identifies which encoding symbols that packet contains. Fourth, the FEC Object Transmission Information includes details needed to decode, such as the total object length and how the object is split into source blocks.

The FEC Encoding ID and FEC Object Transmission Information can be sent in packet headers, in separate session-control packets, or out-of-band. The FEC Payload ID MUST be in every data packet.
sections.eli5: A message needs four labels: which math you are using (Encoding ID), which version of that math (Instance ID), which repair pieces are in this packet (Payload ID), and how to decode the whole message (Transmission Information).

sections.title: Fully-Specified and Under-Specified Schemes
sections.content:
RFC 3452 distinguishes between two types of FEC schemes. A Fully-Specified FEC scheme is completely defined in an IETF RFC, so independent implementors can build compatible encoders and decoders. A Under-Specified FEC scheme leaves some details unspecified, either because a full specification is not available or because a party owns proprietary algorithms they will not disclose.

The RFC reserves FEC Encoding IDs 0-127 for Fully-Specified schemes and 128-255 for Under-Specified schemes. For Under-Specified schemes, an (FEC Encoding ID, FEC Instance ID) tuple uniquely identifies the scheme, and the owner must be able to provide information on how to obtain it. All Under-Specified schemes sharing an FEC Encoding ID MUST use the same FEC Payload ID format.
sections.eli5: Some math is published and anyone can implement it (Fully-Specified). Some math is kept secret but identified by a number so commercial software can use it (Under-Specified).

sections.title: Packet Headers and Block Structures
sections.content:
RFC 3452 specifies two main FEC Encoding ID values. Encoding ID 128 covers Small Block, Large Block, and Expandable FEC codes. Its FEC Payload ID contains a 32-bit Source Block Number and a 32-bit Encoding Symbol ID, identifying which block the symbols come from and which specific symbols are in the packet.

Encoding ID 129 is for Small Block Systematic FEC codes, where source blocks are at most 65536 source symbols. Its FEC Payload ID includes Source Block Number, Source Block Length (16 bits), and Encoding Symbol ID. The block length field lets the sender dynamically change block sizes and communicate them with low overhead in the packet header.

Both schemes require the FEC Object Transmission Information to specify the total object length, how the object is partitioned into blocks, and the maximum number of encoding symbols. All encoding symbols in a block MUST be the same length.
sections.eli5: Packets say which block of the message they carry (Source Block Number) and which repair pieces they are (Encoding Symbol ID). Some schemes also include the block size in the header so it can change.

sections.title: From Building Block to Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 3452 is a building block, not a complete protocol. It describes what information is needed but not out-of-band communication methods, session control, or congestion control. Congestion control MUST be provided by another building block; RFC 2357 specifies the requirements. Complete protocols that use this FEC building block must specify how feedback packets (if used) are formatted and what FEC repair information they contain.

The RFC is Experimental because it was waiting for adequate congestion control schemes to be developed. It has been superseded by RFC 5052 ("The Use of Forward Error Correction (FEC) in Reliable Multicast Transmission") and RFC 5445 with more complete specifications. New implementations should use those RFCs.
sections.eli5: This RFC describes the math for sending repair pieces, but it is not a complete recipe for sending data. Newer RFCs (5052 and 5445) describe complete protocols that use this idea.
